# On Langlands Conjectures: Probabilistic Methods

Nick Polson and Vadim Sokolov. Independently published, 2026. Edition 1, version 1.2.0. DOI: [10.5281/zenodo.23503453](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23503453).

This monograph asks what probability can contribute to the Langlands programme, and answers on two sides. The first is a limitation, proved in the opening chapter: no argument that sees only the limiting distribution of Frobenius data can detect automorphy, because equidistribution is a consequence of functoriality, not a route to it. The second is what probability does supply: consequences of the conjectures, calibration against data, and probabilistic reformulations.

The book covers Weyl's criterion and the Sato Tate law, random matrix models of the zeros of L functions, Hecke operators as random walks on Bruhat Tits trees, hitting times on supersingular isogeny graphs, and Bayesian inference for Sato Tate groups. At its centre is the Thorin framework: for a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL(n) over the rationals, the generalized Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to the statement that the reciprocal of an even completion of its L function is the Laplace transform of a generalized gamma convolution. Later chapters turn the same devices on reciprocity, Fermat's last theorem, random integers and the Poisson Dirichlet law, Hecke characters, Maass forms, Calegari's theorems on even representations and potential modularity, and the crossing probabilities of critical percolation, whose threshold law is, up to normalisation, the Mellin transform of the completed L function of an elliptic curve. These are reformulations: no new case of reciprocity and no Riemann hypothesis is proved.

Results new to the book include the limit of the normalised Kemeny constants of supersingular isogeny graphs, the Thorin criteria for the generalized Riemann hypothesis and for the Ramanujan conjecture, an extreme value representation of the L functions of multiplicative eta products, the Gamma process limit of the Frobenius labelled factorisation of a random integer, and a consistency theorem for the Bayesian identification of Sato Tate groups. Open computational problems close every chapter, and the scripts and data behind the numbers are in the repository.

## Main results

- [Equidistribution does not determine automorphy](RESULTS.md#equidistribution_does_not_determine_automorphy) (Proposition 1.5, page 7): Sato Tate equidistribution of a sequence indexed by the primes cannot certify that it comes from a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL(2) with trivial central character, because altering such a sequence on an infinite set of primes of density zero leaves the limiting empirical averages of all continuous functions unchanged but, by Ramakrishnan's refinement of strong multiplicity one, makes it nonautomorphic, and continuum many equidistributed sequences are not automorphic.
- [Limit of the normalised Kemeny constants of supersingular isogeny graphs](RESULTS.md#kemeny_constant_supersingular_isogeny_graphs_limit) (Theorem 10.6, page 151): As the characteristic grows through primes congruent to 1 modulo 12, with the prime isogeny degree fixed, the mean time for simple random walk on a supersingular isogeny graph to hit a uniformly random curve is asymptotic to the number of vertices times the expected number of visits of simple random walk on the regular tree of the same degree to its starting point, so about twice the number of vertices for 2 isogenies.
- [Thorin criteria for the generalized Riemann hypothesis of automorphic L functions](RESULTS.md#thorin_criteria_generalized_riemann_hypothesis_automorphic) (Theorem 14.8, page 220): The generalized Riemann hypothesis for the L function of a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL(n) over the rationals, and the Riemann hypothesis for zeta, are each equivalent to several positivity statements, among them that the reciprocal of the self dual completion, read in the squared variable, is the Laplace transform of a generalized gamma convolution whose Thorin measure sits at the squared ordinates of the zeros, and a Hankel criterion computable from central derivatives; the theorem is an equivalence that extends the first author's 2018 paper, and it proves no case of either hypothesis.
- [Thorin criterion for the Ramanujan Petersson conjecture at a prime](RESULTS.md#ramanujan_petersson_local_thorin_criterion) (Corollary 15.4, page 238): For a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL(2) over the rationals with trivial central character, the Ramanujan Petersson conjecture at an unramified prime (outside the degenerate case of trace 2) holds exactly when the reciprocal of the symmetrised Euler factor, read in the squared variable, is the Laplace transform of a probability law, which is then a generalized gamma convolution whose Thorin measure is a periodic comb (Ramanujan is local Thorin, as the generalized Riemann hypothesis is global Thorin); the corollary is an equivalence and proves no case of the conjecture.
- [Thorin structure of passage times of the Hecke walk on the regular tree](RESULTS.md#thorin_structure_hecke_walk_passage_times_tree) (Theorem 15.15, page 246): The first time that continuous time simple random walk on a regular tree (the Hecke walk, on the Bruhat Tits tree when the degree is a prime plus one) reaches distance n from its start is a generalized gamma convolution whose Thorin atoms, given by the zeros of the sphere polynomials of the tree, lie in the Kesten band and follow the arcsine law as n grows, with an exact mean, a variance linear in n and a central limit theorem; Thorin support in the Kesten band is the random walk form of the Ramanujan bound, and this unconditional theorem about the tree proves no case of the Ramanujan conjecture for automorphic forms.
- [Gamma process limit of the Frobenius labelled factorisation of a random integer](RESULTS.md#frobenius_labelled_factorisation_gamma_process_limit) (Theorem 20.18, page 350): As the parameter of a zeta distributed random integer decreases to one, the logarithms of its prime power factors, multiplied by the parameter minus one and labelled by any equidistributed sequence of points such as Frobenius classes or Sato Tate angles, converge in law to the jumps of a standard Gamma subordinator carrying independent labels drawn from the equidistribution law, and the labelled logarithm converges in law to a Gamma random measure, so that equidistribution becomes a Gamma process.
- [Extreme value representation of L functions of eta products](RESULTS.md#extreme_value_representation_of_eta_product_l_functions) (Theorem 29.7, page 541): For every eta product, that is every product of the functions eta(m tau) raised to nonnegative integer powers r_m with the sum of m r_m equal to 24 (the thirty multiplicative eta products among them), the L function is entire and equals at every complex point the expectation of a regularised incomplete gamma function evaluated at an explicit maximum of exponential clocks, so its values at positive real points are probabilities strictly between zero and one that increase strictly to one.
- [Consistency of Bayes factors under equidistribution](RESULTS.md#consistency_of_bayes_factors_under_equidistribution) (Theorem 31.1, page 571): For any deterministic sequence, such as normalised Frobenius traces, that is equidistributed for a true law with finitely many atoms and finite Kullback Leibler divergence from one candidate law, and with a log likelihood ratio continuous off the atoms, the clipped log Bayes factor between two candidate laws is asymptotically linear in the number of observations, and as the clipping level grows its slope tends to the difference of the divergences of the true law from the two candidates, with no independence assumed.

All 194 catalogued results, with statements and status, are in [RESULTS.md](RESULTS.md). To credit a result, cite Polson and Sokolov (2026), *On Langlands Conjectures: Probabilistic Methods*, edition 1, with the number of the result.

## Building

The source is LaTeX in `book/`, built with pdflatex; latexmk also runs makeindex, and the bibliography is the hand written `thebibliography` of `book/chapters/bibliography.tex`, so there is no BibTeX step:

```sh
cd book
latexmk -pdf main.tex
```

`book/main.tex` holds the whole preamble (packages, theorem styles, notation macros) and inputs the chapters in book order; the files in `book/chapters/` hold content only. File names follow an earlier plan of the book, not the printed numbers: `ch07.tex` is Chapter 9, the chapters inserted later have lettered names (`ch06b.tex`) or names after their subject (`ch_recip.tex`), and the build's table of contents gives the mapping. `book/bookmeta.tex`, generated from `book.yaml`, gives the copyright page its version, year and DOI. The figures are in `book/figs/`. The book is typeset at the 7 x 10 in trim of the paperback, and the same layout is the published PDF; the print edition sold on Amazon is the same source with the paperback ISBN on its copyright page. `python3 ../book/cover.py PAGES`, run in `cover/` with matplotlib, draws the cover wrap `cover_wrap.pdf` for a page count.

## Code and data

Appendix B of the book, "Code for the Computations", prints the core routines, lists every script with the chapters that use its results, and says how the scripts run, which were rerun and what the reruns gave. The scripts and the JSON files of their results are in these folders:

| Folder | Contents |
|---|---|
| top level | The stage scripts `stage1.py` to `stage9d.py` with their JSON files, behind most of Chapters 4 to 16 and 28 to 30, and the figure scripts `figs.py`, `figs2.py`, `fig3.py`, `fig3b.py`, `fig9.py`, `fig_parabola10b.py`, `stage5fig.py` and `stage7fig.py`. They ran in a sandbox: they hardcode its path `/home/claude/langlands/` and read arrays that were not kept, so they do not run as they stand. |
| `code/` | The same scripts in a portable layout, each run from its own folder with the shared files in `code/work/`: `book_build/` (the stage and figure scripts, `compute.py` and `etacheck.py`), `book_figscripts/` (the scripts of six figures that have none at the top level), `ch17_reciprocity/`, `ch17_gamma_process/` and `ch18_hitting/` (copies of `recip/` and `hitting/`; the folder names follow an earlier numbering of the chapters, now 20 and 21), and `open_problems/` and `scratch/` (pilot computations; none is quoted in the book, except `scratch/dbg8.py` in Appendix B). |
| `beta/` | `fig_beta.py`, the two figures of Chapter 18 (Chapters 17 and 18 came without scripts; their text says how their numbers were computed). |
| `scholze/` | Chapter 19: signed Thorin densities by Stieltjes inversion and zero counts by the argument principle. |
| `recip/` | Chapter 20: Frobenius data for the primes below 10^7, Gamma process laws, heat traces and the figures. |
| `hitting/` | Chapter 21: isogeny graphs, critical groups and Smith forms through PARI/GP, hitting rates, explosion times and exit laws. |
| `flt/` | Chapter 22: Wilton's congruence, Thorin measures of elliptic curves and Eisenstein congruences. |
| `laplace/code/` | Chapter 23: the three faces of the weight one form of level 23, Cauchy smoothing over the zeros of zeta, the Thorin tail, and in `splines/` the Good and Gaskins estimate. |
| `pd/code/` | Chapter 24: random integers, the Poisson Dirichlet law and Mertens constants per Chebotarev class. |
| `gl1/code/` | Chapter 25: Gaussian primes and Hecke angles, Mertens and Landau constants modulo 4, the zeros of L(s, chi_4) and the complex multiplication test for the curve 32a2. |
| `maass/code/` | Chapter 26: prime geodesics of the modular surface, Brownian motion on it, the Eichler Selberg trace formula and Serre's vertical Sato Tate law at p = 2. |
| `percolation/scripts/` | Chapter 27: the crossing threshold of critical percolation and the curve y^2 = x^3 + 1, with mpmath alone: tests of hyperbolic complete monotonicity, the continued Laplace transform with its real zeros and an argument principle count, the Lévy function, the cumulants and zero sums, the reciprocal density, and the Hankel and Prony recovery of the zeros. The figures of the chapter came without a script. |

The scripts are Python 3 with numpy, scipy, mpmath, sympy, networkx and matplotlib, and many use PARI/GP through cypari2 (the reruns used PARI 2.15). Several read an array file that another script writes and that is not kept here, such as the `data.npz` of each folder's `data.py`, which therefore runs first; Appendix B gives the order. Most figure scripts write into a folder `figs/` below their own, which must exist; those of `gl1/code/` and `maass/code/` write into `../book/figs/`, a path of the layout in which they ran. The scripts of Chapters 25 and 26 have not been rerun. The reruns were made on the Hopper cluster of George Mason University.

Not published here: the drafts of the chapters as first written, with their standalone builds, and the review and verification records of the manuscript.

The scripts and data files are under the MIT license (`code/LICENSE`, which covers every code folder of this repository); the text, figures and PDF of the book are under CC BY 4.0 (`LICENSE`).
